overview.body:
**Midir** (*midir*) ​— Underworld, Fairy ‌King · ‌Judge — is ​the lord of ​the síd ​of Brí Léith, ​the Otherworld mound ​by Ardagh ‌in Longford, and ​the central figure ​of *Tochmarc ‌Étaíne*, the Wooing ​of Étaín: foster-father ‌of [[aengus|Óengus]], ​husband of Fuamnach ‌and of [[etain|Étaín]], ​and the ​player of the ​most consequential board ​game in ​Irish literature — ‌the fidchell match ​at Tara in ‌which he ​won Étaín from ‌Eochaid Airem, high ​king of ‌Ireland.[^1]

The tradition ​styles him Mídir ‌the Proud, ​and the handbooks ​gloss his name, ‌with due ‌caution, as 'judge' ‌— a reading ​that fits ​a god whose ‌whole dossier is ​a wager ​conducted like a ‌verdict: he loses ​stake after ​stake until the ‌board is set ​for the one ‌prize he ​came for.[^2] The ​genealogical tradition makes ​him a ​son of [[dagda|the ‌Dagda]], and *De ‌Gabáil in ​t-Sída* makes his ‌fosterage of Óengus ​the hinge ​on which the ‌division of the ‌síd-mounds turns.[^3]

‌PuniCodex restores the ‌name as **Midir** ​— identical ‌to the ASCII ​input, because normalized ​Old Irish ​writes no diacritic ‌in this name; ​the fada of ​modern editorial ​Mídir is a ‌convention, not the ​manuscript norm. ​The mechanical rule ​therefore places it ‌in Tier ​2: nothing distinctive ‌is lost in ​transit, a ‌statement about orthography ​and never about ‌the god. ‌No domain is ​claimed: the plain-ASCII ​**midir.com** is ​registered to a ​third party outside ‌the collection ‌and is watched ​for release.[^1]

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Midir.
Hull, Vernam, ed. and trans., 'De Gabáil in t-Sída', Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 19 (1933).

the-name.body:
The theonym ​is attested in ‌Old and ‌Middle Irish as ​**Midir**, the spelling ​Bergin and ​Best print from ​Lebor na hUidre; ​many modern ‌editors add the ​fada — **Mídir** ​— to mark ‌the long ​vowel, an editorial ‌convention rather than ​the manuscript ‌norm.[^1] The handbooks ​keep his standing ​epithet: Mídir the ​Proud, the ​proud host of ​the síd of ‌Brí Léith.[^2]

​The etymology is ‌genuinely open, and ​this edition ‌keeps it open. ​The reading the ‌reference works register ​derives the ‌name from the ​root *med-*, 'to ​judge, to ‌measure, to rule' ‌— Old Irish ‌*midithir*, 'judges', is ​the comparand ​— yielding a ‌name that would ​suit the ​god of the ‌wager down to ​the ground. ​The derivation is ‌hedged in the ​dictionaries themselves, and ‌the hedge ​is part of ​the record.[^3]

The ​ASCII form ​*midir* loses nothing, ‌because the normalized ‌Old Irish ​spelling is already ‌plain Latin letters; ​the restoration is ​therefore a ‌matter of canonical ‌reference, not rescued ‌diacritics, and ‌the name is ​classified Tier 2 ‌by the project's ​mechanical rule.

​The letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **m** ‌→ **M** ​— Same, capitalized
​- **i** → ​**i** — ‌Same
- **d** ​→ **d** — ​Same
- **i** ​→ **i** ‌— Same
- ​**r** → **r** ‌— Same

​The project holds ‌no domain for ​this name: **midir.com** ‌is registered ‌to a third ​party outside the ​PuniCodex collection ​and is watched ​for release. The ‌temple lives ‌at its canonical ​lexicon address.

sources.citation: Dictionary of the Irish Language (Dublin: Royal Irish Academy, 1913–76; electronic ed. eDIL 2019), s.v. Midir.
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Midir.
Vendryes, Joseph (gen. ed.), Lexique étymologique de l'irlandais ancien (Dublin: Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1959–96), s.v. med-; eDIL, s.v. midithir.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/ˈmʲiː.ðʲɪɾʲ/** — Old ​Irish Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

​- **M-** — ​Slender (palatalized) ​bilabial nasal [mʲ], ‌the tongue arched ​toward the ​hard palate; Old ‌Irish distinguished slender ​from broad ‌consonants throughout
- ​**-í-** — Long ‌close front ​[iː], the long ​vowel modern ​editors mark with ​a fada
- ​**-d-** — ‌Lenited dental [ð], ​the soft voiced ‌'th' of ​English *this*; the ‌orthography writes a ​plain d
‌- **-ir** — ​Short unstressed [ɪ] ‌closing in ​a slender (palatalized) ​tap [ɾʲ]

For ‌the modern ‌speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: ​'MEE-thir' — a ​long 'ee', the ‌soft 'th' ​of *this* for ​the d, and ‌a whispered ​palatal r at ​the end; the ‌modern Irish ​Mídír keeps essentially ‌this sound.

Kindred ​and historical ​forms of the ​name:

- **Old ​Irish** — ‌Midir of Brí ‌Léith; the genealogical ​tradition makes ‌him a son ​of the ​Dagda
- **Manuscript ‌form** — Midir, ‌as printed ‌by Bergin and ‌Best from Lebor ​na hUidre
‌- **Modern Irish** ​— Mídír, with ​the fada ​marking the long ‌vowel
- **Epithet** ​— Mídir ​the Proud, the ​handbooks' standing rendering ‌of his ​style[^2]
- **Anglicized** ​— none: ​unlike Angus, the ‌name never wore ​down into ‌a living given ​name

Midir is ‌Tier 2 ​because the restoration ‌preserves nothing ASCII ‌loses: the ​letters of the ​manuscript form are ​the letters ​of the keyboard. ‌The capital alone ‌marks the ​temple form.

sources.citation: Thurneysen, Rudolf, A Grammar of Old Irish, trans. D. A. Binchy and Osborn Bergin (Dublin: Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1946), on lenition and the broad/slender system.
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Midir.

domains.body:
**Midir** is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ‌'Underworld, Fairy King' ​— two ​terms that ​map onto the ​two halves ​of his ‌dossier, the mound ​he rules ​and the ‌host he commands.[^1]

​### Underworld

‌The Irish ​Otherworld enters this ‌dossier from ​below: Brí ​Léith is a ​hollow hill, ​a síd, ​and the tale's ‌great set-piece ​is its excavation ‌— Eochaid's ​host digging ‌up the mounds ​of Ireland ‌one by ​one until the ‌war of ​spades reached ​Midir's own roof. ‌The underworld ‌here is ‌not a place ​of punishment ​but of ‌plenty and music, ​the wondrous ​land of ‌Midir's song to ​Étaín, hidden ​under a ‌real Longford hill.[^1]

​### Fairy ‌King

The ​síd-lord is the ​medieval original ​of the ​later fairy king: ‌the proud ‌host of ​the mound, master ‌of glamour ​and shape-changing, ​whose bargains bind ‌mortal kings. ‌The continuity ‌from Midir's court ‌to the ​fairy-faith of ‌the Irish countryside ​is the ​tradition's own, ​documented in the ‌folklore collections ​long after the ​manuscripts.[^2]

### ​The Wager ‌as Judgment

The ​handbooks' cautious ​gloss of ​the name — ‌'judge' — ​meets the ‌tale at the ​fidchell board: ‌the game ​at Tara is ‌conducted like ‌a court, ​the stakes schooling ​the king's ​greed until ​the final stake ‌is named ‌and the ​verdict lands.[^3]

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.
Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Mídir, síd.
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Midir.

symbols.body:
Midir's ​attributes are ‌the instruments ‌of ​his patience ​— a ​board, ​a chain, ​a thorn, ‌a ​hill, and ​a riddle ‌of faces:[^1]

​- ‌**The fidchell ​board** — ‌The ​game of ​kings played ​at ​Tara: patience ​staked as ‌strategy, ​and a ‌wager that ​was ‌really a ​judgment
- ‌**The ​silver chain** ‌— The ​link ​between the ‌two swans ‌that rose ‌through ​Tara's smoke-hole: ​the bond ‌the ​high king's ​host could ‌not ​break
- ​**The sloe-thorn** ‌— ​The flying ‌thorn that ​put ​out his ​eye at ​the ‌Brug and ‌set the ​whole ‌wooing in ​motion; Dían ​Cécht healed ‌the ‌wound
- ‌**Brí Léith** ‌— ​His síd ‌by Ardagh ​in ​Longford, the ​mound the ‌Dindsenchas ​names as ​his and ​the ‌host of ​Ireland dug ​open ​to take ‌Étaín back[^2]
​- ‌**The fifty ​women in ‌one likeness** ​— ‌The riddle ‌of resemblance ​at ​the mound's ​surrender: the ​Otherworld's ‌coldest answer ‌to the ​spade[^1]

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.
Stokes, Whitley, ed. and trans., 'The Prose Tales in the Rennes Dindsenchas', Revue Celtique 15–16 (1894–95), s.v. Brí Léith.

mythology.body:
Midir's mythology is a ​single long courtship told in two ‌lifetimes, preserved entire in *Tochmarc Étaíne* ‌— the fullest Otherworld dossier in ​the Irish corpus.[^1]

### The Sloe and ​the Bride-Price (Tochmarc Étaíne I)

Midir ​of Brí Léith, foster-father of [[aengus|Óengus]], ​came to Brú na Bóinne to ​visit his fosterling; a sloe-thorn sprang ‌from the boys' hurling-play and put out ​his eye, and he stayed a ​year in the mound while Dían ‌Cécht made him whole. For his ​reward he named [[etain|Étaín]] Echraide, daughter of ‌Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland. ​Óengus won her from her father ‌Ailill mac Máta, king of the ​Ulaid, by performing the demanded labors ​— twelve plains cleared, twelve rivers led ​to the sea — with the ​Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir ​brought her home to Brí Léith.[^1]

‌### The Fly in the Crystal Bower ​(Tochmarc Étaíne II)

Fuamnach, Midir's first ‌wife and foster-daughter of Bresal the ​druid, struck her rival with a ‌rod of scarlet quicken-tree: Étaín became a ​pool of water, a worm, and ‌a purple fly. The fly went ​with Midir for seven years and ‌he knew her in her shape; ​she found refuge in Óengus's crystal bower ​at the Brug until Fuamnach's wind ‌swept her across Ireland for seven ‌years more, to fall into the ‌cup of Étar's wife at the Bay ​of Cíú and be born again ​a thousand and twelve years after ‌her first birth — Étaín, daughter ​of Étar.[^1]

### The Long Game ​at Tara (Tochmarc Étaíne III)

In her ‌second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, ​high king at Tara. Midir came ​first in the likeness of the ‌king's love-sick brother Ailill Anglonnach, lying beside ​her three nights without touching her; ‌then he revealed himself, and she ​answered that she would not go ​without her husband's leave. He took the ​leave at the fidchell board: game ​after game he lost, paying stakes ‌without stint, until the final stake ‌was named — an embrace and ​a kiss from Étaín — and Midir ‌won. When the month's deferral was ​out he appeared in the midst ​of the barred and guarded hall, ‌sang to her the invitation to the ‌wondrous land, and the two rose ‌through the smoke-hole as two swans ‌linked by a silver chain.[^1]

### ​The Fifty Women in One Likeness ‌(Tochmarc Étaíne III)

Eochaid answered with the ​spade, digging up the síd-mounds of ​Ireland until the host stood over ​Brí Léith. Midir came to the ‌parley; fifty women in Étaín's exact likeness ​came out of the mound, and ​the king was told to choose. ​He chose his own daughter, born ‌to Étaín in the síd and hidden ​in her mother's likeness — the ​unwitting union from which came Mess ​Búachalla, grandmother of Conaire Mór. When ‌Midir revealed the deception he returned ​the true Étaín, and kept the last ‌word.[^1]

### The Foster-Father of the ​Young God (De Gabáil in t-Sída)

‌Behind the wooing stands the fosterage: ​when the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of ‌Ireland, Óengus was away with Midir ‌at Brí Léith and received nothing ​— the absence that led to ​the day-and-night quibble and the winning ​of Brú na Bóinne. The tradition ties ​the two mounds together from the ‌beginning: the young god reared at ‌Brí Léith, the proud god's eye ​healed at the Brug.[^2]

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.
Hull, Vernam, ed. and trans., 'De Gabáil in t-Sída', Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 19 (1933).

syncretism.body:
Midir ​has no ‌cross-border witness ‌of his ​own, and ​the honest ​comparison ​is typological ​rather than ‌genetic. No ​Gaulish altar ​names him ‌and ​no scholar ‌has proposed ​one; where ‌the Dagda ​can be ​set ​beside Sucellos ​on the ​strength of ‌club and ​cauldron, ‌Midir's dossier ​— the ‌wager, the ​hunted bride, ‌the mound ​that ‌is a ​court — ​belongs to ‌the Otherworld-king ‌figure-type that ‌Mac ​Cana and ​Sjoestedt trace ‌through the ​Celtic materials ​without anchoring ‌it ​to any ​single epigraphic ‌god.[^1]

Within ​Ireland his ‌structural kin ​are ​the síd-lords ​of the ​neighboring tales: ‌Bodb Derg ‌of the ​Munster ‌síde, who ​answers the ​Dagda's search ‌in the ‌*Aislinge Óenguso*, ‌and ‌[[manannan|Manannán]], the ​sea-going master ‌of the ​Otherworld's glamour.[^2] ​The Welsh ​corpus ‌offers only ​a functional ​parallel — ​[[arawn|Arawn]], the ‌lord ​of Annwn ​who likewise ​binds a ‌mortal king ​by a ‌bargain ​with a ‌hidden edge ​— and ‌the parallel ‌is a ​pattern, ​not a ​pedigree. The ​comparisons instruct; ‌none of ‌them identifies ​him.

sources.citation: Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970); Sjoestedt, Marie-Louise, Gods and Heroes of the Celts, trans. Myles Dillon (London: Methuen, 1949).
Shaw, Francis, ed., Aislinge Óenguso (Dublin: Browne and Nolan, 1934).

cultural-legacy.body:
Midir's ​afterlife is ‌the afterlife ‌of *Tochmarc ​Étaíne* itself, ​the tale ​that never ​let him ​go. P. ‌W. Joyce ​carried 'The ​Wooing of ‌Etain' into ​modern English ‌in *Old ​Celtic Romances* ‌(1879), and ​Lady Gregory ​made the ​fidchell game ​and the ​swans part ‌of the ​Celtic revival's ‌furniture in ​*Gods and ‌Fighting Men* ​(1904).[^1] James ‌Stephens gave ​the story ‌its strangest ​modern retelling ​in *In ‌the Land ‌of Youth* ‌(1924), where ​Midir's arrival ​at Tara ‌is staged ​as high ​comedy turning ‌to awe.[^2]

​Bergin and ​Best's edition ‌in ​*Ériu* (1938) ‌fixed the ​text for ​scholarship, and ​Jeffrey Gantz's ​Penguin translation ‌(1981) put ‌the whole ​dossier on ‌the general ​reader's shelf, ​where it ‌has stayed: ‌the fidchell ‌game is ‌now the ​standard citation ‌whenever Irish ​literature wants ​to prove ​that its ‌gods play ​a longer ​game than ​its kings.[^3] ‌The name ​itself took ​no second ​path — ‌no Angus, ​no Brigit: ‌Midir never ​became a ‌given name, ​a place, ‌or a ‌pub, and ​remains what ​the manuscripts ​made him, ​a proper ‌noun with ‌a single ​bearer.

sources.citation: Joyce, P. W., Old Celtic Romances (London: C. Kegan Paul, 1879), 'The Wooing of Etain'; Gregory, Lady Augusta, Gods and Fighting Men (London: John Murray, 1904).
Stephens, James, In the Land of Youth (London: Macmillan, 1924).
Gantz, Jeffrey, trans., Early Irish Myths and Sagas (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1981).

archaeology.body:
Midir is ​a textual ‌god — ‌no ogham ​stone names him ​and no ​votive inscription ​invokes him — ​but both ‌halves of ​his mythic ​geography are real ‌and visitable. ​Brí Léith ‌is a ​hill by Ardagh ‌in County ​Longford, the ​mound the Dindsenchas ​names as ​his síd, ​and the ‌surrounding Longford bogland ​preserves one ‌of the ​showpiece monuments ‌of the Irish ​Iron Age: ‌the Corlea ​Trackway, a massive ‌oak togher ​across the ​bog a ‌few miles south ‌of Ardagh, ‌excavated under ​Barry Raftery ​and fixed by ‌dendrochronology to ​148–147 BCE ​— a road ‌of the ​very centuries ​in which ‌the síd-lord's landscape ​was being ‌imagined.[^1]

The ​tale's other ​stage is Tara ​in County ​Meath, where ‌the earthworks of ‌Ráith na ​Rí, the ‌Forrad, and ​the long banquet-hall ​trench called ‌Tech Midchúarta ‌still ridge ‌the hill on ‌which Eochaid ​Airem kept ‌his court and ​lost his ​wager.[^2] The ​manuscript witnesses ‌are exact: *Tochmarc ​Étaíne* is ​preserved, incompletely, ​in the ‌twelfth-century Lebor na ​hUidre (RIA ​MS 23 ​E 25) and ‌completed in ​the fifteenth-century ‌Yellow Book ​of Lecan, the ‌twin bases ​of Bergin ‌and Best's ‌edition; the companion ​*Aislinge Óenguso* ​survives in ​the fifteenth-century British ​Library MS ‌Egerton 1782, ‌the basis ​of Shaw's.[^3]

sources.citation: Raftery, Barry, on the Corlea Trackway excavations (University College Dublin, 1984–91) and its dendrochronological date of 148–147 BCE.
Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Tara, Brí Léith.
Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), introduction, on the manuscripts.

meditation.body:
Midir is ​the god of ‌the long ‌game, and the ​tradition tells you ​so in ​his name before ​it tells you ​in his ‌story: the handbooks ​gloss it, cautiously, ​as judge ‌— and a ​judge is exactly ‌what a ​wager needs. Watch ‌how he plays ​Eochaid. He ​loses, and loses, ​and pays without ​stint, because ​the losses are ‌the lesson: the ​king is ‌being taught that ​the man across ‌the board ​can afford anything, ‌that the stakes ​are a ‌language, and that ​the only sentence ​being written ‌is the last ‌one. When the ‌final stake ​is named — ​an embrace, a ‌kiss — ​the game has ​already been won ‌for a ​month. The fidchell ​board is a ‌court, and ​the house always ‌already holds the ​verdict.[^1]

That ​patience is the ​Otherworld's whole tempo. ​A mortal ‌wooing is measured ‌in seasons; Midir's ​spans a ‌thousand and twelve ​years, two births ​of the ‌same woman, and ‌a war of ‌spades against ‌his own roof ​— and he ‌never hurries, ​because time is ​the one currency ​his kind ‌does not spend. ​His foster-son [[aengus|Óengus]] ​parses time ​into a loophole ‌and holds a ​mound on ​a day without ​a term; the ‌foster-father plays ​time into a ‌stake and holds ​a woman ‌across two lifetimes. ​Between them the ‌síd of ‌Ireland teaches the ​same doctrine: the ​hollow hills ​do not take ​what they want. ‌They wait ‌until the wanting ​itself concedes.

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.

irish-cycles.body:
Midir belongs ​to the ‌Mythological Cycle, ‌and his ​dossier is ​one of ​its cornerstones: ​*Tochmarc Étaíne*, the ​Wooing of ‌Étaín, is ​preserved, incompletely, ​in the ‌twelfth-century Lebor ​na hUidre ‌and completed in ​the Yellow ‌Book of ​Lecan, and ​it gives ​him the ​fullest Otherworld narrative ​in the ‌language — ​the eye ‌and the ​bride-price, the ‌fly and ​the bower, the ‌fidchell game, ​and the ‌digging of ​the síds.[^1] ​The *Lebor ‌Gabála Érenn* ‌genealogies place him ‌in the ​Dagda's line, ​and the ‌prose *Dindsenchas* ​keeps Brí ​Léith among ‌the storied places ​as his ​mound.[^2]

Around ‌that spine ​the companion ‌tales build ​the foster-father. *De ​Gabáil in ​t-Sída* makes ​his fosterage ‌of [[aengus|Óengus]] ‌the reason ​the young ‌god was absent ​at the ​division of ‌the mounds;[^3] ‌the *Aislinge ‌Óenguso* opens ‌the world ​of the síd-lords ‌among whom ​the fosterling ​moved.[^4] Medieval ​scribes framed ‌the Túatha ​Dé Danann ​as kings and ​wizards of ‌the pre-Milesian ​age, but ​Midir is ​one of ‌the figures the ​euhemerizing frame ‌cannot hold: ​the tale ‌needs him ​to be ‌what he ‌is — the ​proud host ​of the ​hollow hill, ​playing a ‌game no ‌mortal king ​can afford.

welsh-sources.body:
The ​Welsh corpus ‌is silent ‌on ​Midir, and ​the silence ​deserves ​to be ​recorded rather ‌than ​repaired. Neither ​the *Mabinogi* ‌nor the ​wider ‌Brythonic tradition ​preserves a ‌figure ​derived from ​the same ​name, ​and no ​identification of ‌him ​behind any ‌Welsh persona ​has ‌found standing ​in the ‌modern ​handbooks.[^1]

What ‌the comparison ​does ​offer is ‌a functional ‌parallel, and ‌it ​is instructive ​precisely because ‌it ​is not ​a pedigree. ‌[[arawn|Arawn]], ​the lord ​of Annwn ‌in ​the First ‌Branch, is ​the ​Welsh Otherworld ​king who ​likewise ‌binds a ‌mortal ruler ​by ‌a bargain ​whose terms ​hide their ‌edge ‌— the ‌same figure-type, ‌arrived ​at independently. ‌The Welsh ​divine ​families organize ​their Otherworld ‌around ​other names, ​and the ​nearest ‌Welsh parallels ​for Midir's ​patience ​and pride ‌are distributed ​rather ‌than concentrated. ​The honest ‌Celtic comparison ​therefore ‌runs not ‌west to ​Wales ​but inward, ​to the ​síd-lords ‌of the ‌neighboring Irish ​tales.[^2]

sources.citation: Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Mídir.
Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (Hamlyn, 1970), on the Otherworld-king figure-type across the Celtic traditions.

inscriptions.body:
No ​inscription names ‌Midir. **Ogham**, ‌the ​early Irish ​monumental script ​of roughly ​the ​fourth to ‌seventh centuries, ​survives ​on some ‌four hundred ​stones ‌bearing mostly ​personal names ‌in ​formulaic genitives; ​no reading ​of Midir ​has ​been proposed ‌for any ​of ‌them, and ​none would ‌be ​expected — ‌ogham stones ​mark ‌graves and ​boundaries, not ​votive dedications.[^1]

‌Nor ‌does the ‌Gaulish record ​supply ​a comparandum. ‌Where the ​Dagda's ​figure-type finds ‌an epigraphic ​neighbor ​in Sucellos, ‌no altar ​from the ‌Celtic ​provinces has ​been read ​as ​addressed to ‌a counterpart ‌of ​Midir, and ‌no scholar ​has ​proposed one; ‌the Otherworld-king ‌dossier — ‌the ‌wager, the ​hunted bride, ‌the ​mound that ​is a ​court ‌— survives ​as literature ​alone.[^2] ​The epigraphic ‌silence is ​characteristic of ​Irish ​paganism, whose ‌cult left ​place-names ‌and literature ​rather than ‌stone: ​Brí Léith ‌on the ‌map, ​and Tochmarc ​Étaíne in ​the codices, ​are ‌the whole ‌of the ​dedication.

sources.citation: McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam, Maynooth Monographs 4 (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1991).
Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (Hamlyn, 1970); Sjoestedt, Marie-Louise, Gods and Heroes of the Celts, trans. Dillon (1949).

original-script.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval Irish ‌manuscripts in ​the Latin alphabet ​as **Midir** ​— Old Irish ​/ Middle Irish ​in Insular ‌script, attested in ​the great ​codices that preserve ‌Tochmarc Étaíne, ​above all the ‌twelfth-century Lebor ​na hUidre, completed ‌by the ​Yellow Book of ​Lecan.[^1] The ​earlier monumental alphabet, ​ogham, predates ​the manuscript tradition, ‌but no attestation ​of this ‌theonym has ever ​been read ‌on an ogham ​stone; the ‌manuscript form is ​the primary ‌witness.[^2]

The scholarly ​rendering proceeds ​step by step:

‌- Old ‌Irish was written ‌in the ​Latin alphabet using ​Insular minuscule from ‌the early ​medieval period; the ​spelling Midir ‌requires no diacritic.
​- Many ​modern editors add ‌the fada ​and print **Mídir** ‌to mark ​the long vowel ​— an ​editorial convention, not ​the manuscript ‌norm; the project ‌follows the manuscript ​form.
- ‌The medial d ​is lenited ​in pronunciation — ‌[ð], the ‌soft 'th' of ‌*this* — ‌but the orthography ​writes plain ‌d; nothing distinctive ​is lost ​in ASCII.[^3]
- ​The Unicode ‌restoration Midir is ​therefore identical to ​the ASCII ​form apart from ‌the capital; ​the temple form ​is a ​canonical reference, not ‌a rescued ​spelling.

One caution ‌attaches to ​the record: the ‌handbooks' gloss ​'judge' — from ‌*med-*, with ‌Old Irish *midithir*, ​'judges', as the ​comparand — ​is hedged in ​the dictionaries ‌themselves, and this ‌edition keeps ​the hedge.[^4]

sources.citation: Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.
McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam, Maynooth Monographs 4 (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1991).
Thurneysen, Rudolf, A Grammar of Old Irish, trans. Binchy and Bergin (Dublin: DIAS, 1946), on lenition.
Vendryes, Joseph (gen. ed.), Lexique étymologique de l'irlandais ancien (DIAS, 1959–96), s.v. med-; eDIL, s.v. midithir; MacKillop, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology, s.v. Midir.
